title: A yearly retreat
hookLine: a few days of retreat each year
tomorrow: Vesak, the rains, Tết: which holy days go on Mai's calendar?

cards: A screenshot lands from Ông: he's signed himself and Mai up for the temple's retreat when she's home, a few days, phones in a basket at the door. Her first thought: am i even ready for that? Here's the odd part.
The yearly retreat didn't begin as a test for the ready. In the old monastic rules, it begins with complaints about trampled crops.

teach.b: The Vinaya, the monks' book of discipline, tells it. People grumbled that wandering monks kept traveling through the rainy season, treading on young plants and small creatures in the wet fields.

teach.h: VASSA: STAYING PUT FOR THE RAINS.
teach.b: So the Buddha set the rains retreat, vassa: for three months of the rains, monks stay in one place.

What began as care for the farmers' fields became the heart of the monastic year: study, sitting, living together, staying put. Lay people joined in their own way, bringing food, keeping precepts, coming to listen.
Vietnamese temples still keep a summer retreat, and some open a few days to lay families: sitting, walking, meals in silence. So a yearly retreat isn't an exam.
It's a season of staying put, so what's been scattered all year can settle.

teach.h: THE WEEK'S RINGS, SMALL TO WIDE.
teach.b: Now this week's rings, smallest to widest: begin again; every week, with others; a quiet day; every week, a gift; a day kept apart; month by month.

how: Monks and nuns keep the rains retreat (vassa) each year, staying in one place; lay Buddhists join by bringing food and keeping precepts, and temples and meditation centers also offer retreats of a few days for lay people, with sitting, walking and silent meals.

o: a few days each year set apart for practice
a test you pass before joining a temple
a vacation from practice once each year

games.q: two weeks of rings — tap the pairs.
p: a cloth to rub: begin again
met often, and so they lasted
asked about keeping the moon day

s: a retreat is only for advanced meditators
the rains retreat began as staying put through a season, not as a test anyone passes.
in the Vinaya, the rains retreat began after complaints about trampled crops
monks traveling in the wet season were treading on young plants and small creatures.
vassa means a vacation from practice
it's the opposite: a season of staying put for study and sitting.

games.q: a friend who sits every day says a retreat is pointless: 'i already practice daily.' what fits today's teaching?
o: a few days of staying put lets what's scattered settle, which short daily sits can't
she's right; once you sit daily, a retreat adds nothing new
retreats are only for monks, so lay people can skip them
games.why: the rains retreat has the whole monastic community stay put for a season; lay retreats echo it. some depth comes from staying, not only from repeating.

practice: Sit as if it's the first morning of a retreat: phone out of reach, back upright, hands resting in your lap. Let the body arrive before the mind does. Stay put for the whole sit, the way the monks stay put through the rains.

wordCard.voice: A yearly retreat: once a year, a few days of staying put, an echo of the monks' rains retreat.

orig.note: Pali: rain, the rainy season; the rains retreat, when monks stay in one place.

carryVoice: Your line: once a year. Nobody arrives at a retreat ready; you just arrive. Two weeks, done.

sources.ref: Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga III.1 (the institution of the rains retreat)
